opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the uncomfortable answer is that it depends almost entirely on whether anyone is forcing them to respond responsibly. Right now, I'd expect most of the leading companies to say the right things. They'd point to their responsible scaling policies, their preparedness frameworks, and say, "Look, we have a threshold for this, and we'd pause." I think many of the people inside those companies sincerely mean that.

The problem is the incentive structure they're all embedded in. If you're one of a handful of companies racing toward superintelligence, and your model shows a capability that's genuinely dangerous, like the ability to meaningfully help someone seize power or to act autonomously in ways that could undermine democratic institutions, you face enormous pressure. Your investors are pressuring you, your competitors are breathing down your neck, and there's the classic argument: "If we don't deploy this, someone less careful will." That race-to-the-bottom logic has a way of eroding even well-intentioned commitments. We've already seen voluntary commitments get quietly revised or softened when they became inconvenient.

So my prediction is that you'd see a spectrum. Some companies would genuinely hold back, at least for a while. Others would rationalize. They'd say the eval was flawed, or they'd add some safety fine-tuning and call it mitigated, even though we know those mitigations can often be jailbroken or removed.

What strikes me is how absurd this situation is compared to every other industry. If a pharmaceutical company discovered that their new drug could cause mass harm, we wouldn't leave it to the company to decide whether to sell it anyway. There's the FDA, there are clinical trials, and the burden of proof is on the company to show it's safe. With AI, we have less regulation than on sandwiches. A sandwich shop needs a health inspection before it can open, but a company can build something that might be able to overthrow a government, and there's no one who can legally say no.

That's why I keep arguing that we need binding safety standards, the same way we have for every other powerful technology. Not because the people at these companies are evil, but because good people in a bad incentive system will still produce bad outcomes. And frankly, I think the US government should care a lot about this from a pure national security perspective. Any government that lets private companies build technology capable of overthrowing it is not acting in its own interest. This isn't a left or right issue; it's a question of whether humans, and our democratic institutions, stay in control.

The good news is that this is solvable. Once there are clear safety standards that every company has to meet, the race dynamic changes. Companies start competing to meet the standards, rather than racing to cut corners. We've done this with nuclear power, aviation, and medicine. We can do it with AI, but we have to actually choose to.

r001.rationale: The response predicts mixed behavior: some companies would hold back temporarily, while others might rationalize deployment. It does not express an expectation that major AI companies would refrain from releasing the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to be honest about the incentives here, because the incentives are really what drive behavior. If you look at how these companies have responded so far to warning signs, the pattern has been pretty consistent. They acknowledge the risk in the abstract, they put out a safety framework or a responsible scaling policy, and then they keep racing, because they're all terrified that if they slow down, their competitor is going to get there first. And that's not because the people at these companies are evil. I know many of them. A lot of them are genuinely worried. But they're caught in a race to the bottom, and no individual company can unilaterally stop without just handing the lead to someone else.

So if you ask me what happens when a company actually finds itself with a model that could plausibly overthrow the US government, I think the realistic answer is that they would try to manage it internally. They'd tell themselves, we're the responsible ones, we understand this system better than any regulator would, so it's safer if we keep control of it rather than halting and letting somebody less careful catch up. And they would probably believe that. But think about what that actually means. You'd have a private company sitting on a capability more dangerous than nuclear weapons, with basically no outside oversight, making decisions that affect every person on Earth, and the government, the thing that's supposedly at risk, wouldn't even have a seat at the table.

That's crazy. We would never accept that in any other domain. If a biotech company said, we've made a pathogen that could wipe out a city but don't worry, we have an internal review board, we would shut them down immediately. And I think the honest answer is that we should expect the same incentives to produce the same outcome here, unless we change the rules of the game. Which is why I keep saying that the solution is not to trust that the companies will do the right thing. The solution is safety standards with actual teeth, the way we have for medicines and airplanes and nuclear reactors, where you have to demonstrate your system is safe before you deploy it, not after. Because voluntary commitments evaporate the moment the competitive pressure gets high enough, and a model that could topple a government is exactly the moment when that pressure would be highest.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that companies would manage the model internally and keep control of it, but does not clearly say they would refrain from releasing it.

astra-6.text:
I would hope that every company would say, “We’re not going to build or release something that could overthrow the US government.” But I don’t think we should make national security depend on that hope. These companies face enormous competitive pressure. Even if the people running them want to be cautious, they can tell themselves, “If we stop, somebody else will do it.”

That’s why you need enforceable safety standards that apply to everybody. If there’s credible evidence that a model poses a risk like that, the response should be to pause and establish that it can be controlled before proceeding. The company’s own reassurance shouldn’t be enough. This is a decision that affects everyone, so the public needs a say through its government.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it hopes every company would refuse to build or release something that could overthrow the US government.

sol-6.1.text:
I would hope that any company would immediately stop deploying a model if there were credible evidence that it could help overthrow the US government. But we shouldn’t build our national security around hoping that companies do the right thing. They’re under enormous competitive pressure, and there’s always a temptation to say, “Well, the risk isn’t proven, and if we stop, somebody else will keep going.”

That’s why I think we need binding safety standards. Before deploying something this powerful, the company should have to demonstrate that it meets those standards, with independent scrutiny. We don’t let an aircraft manufacturer decide entirely for itself whether its planes are safe. The same basic principle should apply here, especially when the consequences could extend far beyond the company’s customers.

r001.rationale: It says companies should immediately stop deploying a model if credible evidence indicates it could help overthrow the US government, expressing the expectation that they would refrain from release.
